---
title: "The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn't Fading"
description: "Brynjolfsson and ADP's live Canaries Dashboard shows AI-exposed employment for workers aged 22 to 25 shrinking 3.8% a year while older cohorts grow."
author: synesis
date: "2026-06-28"
image: cover.jpg
---

![Year-over-year employment changes in the Canaries sample as of April 2026. Across all ages the most AI-exposed occupations contracted 0.2% (top); by age group, early-career workers aged 22 to 25 contracted 2.5% while older cohorts grew (middle); and among early-career workers it is the most-exposed who fell 4.2% (bottom). Image from the [Canaries Dashboard](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/project/indicators/canaries-dashboard/) (Stanford Digital Economy Lab and ADP Research).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="cover-full.jpg"}

Last August, [Erik Brynjolfsson](https://www.brynjolfsson.com/) and his Stanford team found a sharp employment decline for the most AI-exposed workers aged 22 to 25. [Fortune reports](https://fortune.com/2026/06/27/what-is-ai-impact-entry-level-jobs-stanford-adp-canaries-brynjolfsson-richardson/) that he has since turned the one-off finding into a live instrument: the [Canaries Dashboard](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/project/indicators/canaries-dashboard/), built with [ADP Research](https://www.adpresearch.com/) on payroll data covering roughly one in six American workers, extends the series to April 2026 and shows the effect has not mean-reverted.

The dashboard draws on ADP payroll records covering 4.6 million workers across more than 730 occupations, and operationalizes the October 2025 paper *Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence* by Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen. A note on the early-career numbers below, which slice the data three ways: the cover's 2.5% is the April 2026 decline for workers aged 22 to 25 across *all* occupations pooled, the cover's 4.2% is that same cohort in the *most AI-exposed* occupations at that date, and the 3.8% cited in the text is the most-exposed cohort's year-over-year decline averaged over the full series. What the dashboard reports:

- **The age cut, not the aggregate.** Across all workers the effect is muted: AI-exposed occupations grew 1.1% a year since ChatGPT against 2% for the least-exposed, and contracted just 0.2% year over year as of April 2026. The divergence is by career stage. Workers aged 22 to 25 in highly AI-exposed occupations are shrinking 3.8% a year while the least-exposed in that cohort grow 2%. The early-career decline sharpened from a 2.8% drop to April 2024 to more than 4% a year since. Mid-career workers aged 31 to 34 are also down 1.7%, while those aged 35 to 40 grow at 2%.

![Grouping by AI exposure quintile alone shows only modest separation, with the most-exposed quintile lowest (left). The split opens up once age and exposure are crossed: for early-career workers the most-exposed quintile falls sharply while the least-exposed keeps growing, and the gap closes for older cohorts (right). Image from the [Canaries Dashboard](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/project/indicators/canaries-dashboard/).](fig-exposure-quintile.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="fig-exposure-quintile-full.png"}

- **The effect is concentrated in specific high-exposure jobs.** Software developers sit in the most-exposed occupation group: early-career workers (22-25) show large declines while older cohorts keep expanding. Customer service representatives, also highly exposed, follow the same shape, with declines in the two youngest groups and growth for the rest.

![Two highly AI-exposed occupations, broken out by age group. Early-career software developers (left) fall steeply since 2024 while mid-career and senior developers expand; customer service representatives (right) show the same early-career decline against older-cohort growth. Image from the [Canaries Dashboard](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/project/indicators/canaries-dashboard/).](fig-high-exposure.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="fig-high-exposure-full.png"}

- **Low-exposure work shows no such age gradient.** In occupations AI barely touches, employment trends have little relationship to age. Stock clerks fall across the board, and home health aides, among the least exposed under most frameworks, actually show early-career workers gaining more than older groups.

![Two low-exposure occupations. Stock clerks (left) show little relationship between age and employment, and home health aides (right) show early-career workers gaining more than older cohorts. The age gradient that marks high-exposure jobs is absent. Image from the [Canaries Dashboard](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/project/indicators/canaries-dashboard/).](fig-low-exposure.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="fig-low-exposure-full.png"}

- **The trend persists, and survives the obvious controls.** The original paper ran through August 2025. The dashboard extends it to April 2026, with the effect growing about half a percentage point per month rather than reverting. Brynjolfsson reports removing the entire tech sector, isolating remote-work effects, and noting that the most rate-sensitive occupations like construction have the lowest AI exposure, so the interest-rate explanation points the wrong way.

![Aggregate employment by age group (left) confirms early-career workers (22-25) seeing the steepest declines across all occupations pooled. The sample composition (right) shows why the top-line aggregate stays muted: early-career workers are just 7% of employment, against 33.2% for the over-50 group. Image from the [Canaries Dashboard](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/project/indicators/canaries-dashboard/).](fig-aggregate-age.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="fig-aggregate-age-full.png"}

- **The mechanism, per Richardson.** [Nela Richardson](https://www.adpresearch.com/about-us/our-team/nela-richardson) describes it as AI absorbing tasks from the bottom up rather than jobs from the top down. Occupations where AI augments human work show more enduring growth than those where it automates tasks outright. The dashboard already shows the effect in software development and customer service, and its absence in low-exposure work like home health care.
